newsitem.title: USA: COCOA--Analysts see U.S. Q4 grind up 3.0-5.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: COCOA--Analysts see U.S. Q4 grind up 3.0-5.0 pct.

text.p: U.S. cocoa production in the 1996 fourth quarter is expected to rise because of low world prices and a steady increase in consumer demand for chocolate, industry sources said.
U.S. cocoa grindings -- a key barometer of consumption -- are forecast to rise three to five percent compared to the same year-ago period. The data are due to be released Friday at 0845 EDT/1345 GMT.
"Cocoa use is on the rise and prices are cheap," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka.
"I think consumption has been better than people think," he added.
Spilka estimated the figure would rise three to four percent versus the 1995 fourth-quarter grind of 93,320 tonnes.

Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes also expected the grind to rise modestly in the fourth quarter due to steady growth in consumption, but said it would be difficult to sustain the strong pace of the three previous quarters of 1996.
"I just have not heard of any talk of heavy demand," Ganes said. "I do not think U.S. consumption has reached a new higher plane."

In third-quarter 1996, U.S. grindings rose 7.52 percent to 93,953 tonnes compared to the 1995 third quarter. In second-quarter 1996, the grind was up 4.85 pct on the year-ago period, while first-quarter grindings rose 0.26 percent.

Disappointing European fourth-quarter grind data could in turn point to a mediocre U.S. fourth-quarter grind number, Ganes said. "With the European numbers, why would we be up five to 10 percent?" she asked.
While many sources said the U.S. grindings are likely to echo the slowdown in Europe, no one expects them to come close to the huge decline seen in the German grind.
German 1996 fourth-quarter grindings fell 21.2 percent to 56,254.7 tonnes compared to the same 1995 period. Analysts had forecast a decline of only two percent.

The Dutch grind rose 3.9 percent in the fourth quarter to 97,273 tonnes, just shy of analysts' projections for a five percent rise. The fourth-quarter grind in the U.K. fell 3.3 percent on the year to 45,147 tonnes, but still was below analysts' predictions for a drop of as much as 10 percent.
However, some analysts, who believe domestic consumption has been stagnant, said the 1996 U.S. fourth-quarter grind was likely to struggle to break even.

"There has not been any real data indicating a strong pickup in consumption," Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson said. "I think it is likely to be three to four percent lower than a year ago."
A possible build in manufacturer inventories following strong grinds in 1996 could also signal a lower figure in this year's fourth quarter, some market participants said.
"We have seen good grinds the first three quarters, but a buildup of finished product may tail it off," a trader said.
Additionally, industry sources will be watching for a downward revision to last year's fourth-quarter grind.
In reporting the 1995 third-quarter results, Chocolate Manufacturers Association revised its year earlier figures by nearly eight percent.
